prompt: Write an essay on whether people learn more from failure or from success.
text:
# Learning From Failure and From Success

People tend to say failure is the best teacher. The saying is popular, but it is only partly right. Failure usually teaches more per event, while success teaches more over a lifetime, and the real question is what each one teaches and whether the learner is paying attention.

## Why failure teaches so much

A failure is surprising. When we expect something to work and it doesn't, we have to ask why. That question pushes us to look for the cause, and we end up with a more accurate picture of how things work. A bridge that stands tells an engineer little about its limits. A bridge that collapses shows exactly where the model was wrong.

Failure also narrows the possibilities. If a cook burns a sauce, she knows that this heat, for this long, is too much. That is concrete information. It also tends to stick, because mistakes carry an emotional charge that routine results lack. Most of us remember the exam we failed more clearly than the ones we passed.

## Why failure is a weaker teacher than it sounds

The lesson only arrives if the learner reads it correctly. Many failures have several possible causes: bad luck, bad timing, a bad plan, or bad execution. People often pick the explanation that protects their pride. A founder whose company folds may blame the market when the real problem was the product. In that case the failure taught nothing, or taught something false.

Failure can also discourage. Repeated early failures lead many learners to quit, or to decide they lack talent. Someone who stops trying learns nothing further. And failure says what doesn't work without saying what does. A hundred ways to fail still leave you short of one way to succeed.

## What success teaches

Success shows you what a working version looks like. A student who solves a problem sees the whole pattern, from start to finish. Success also builds confidence, and confidence makes people willing to attempt harder things. Much skill comes from this loop: do something well, take on something slightly harder, and repeat.

Success has its own danger, though. It hides weak spots. A strategy that worked once may have worked by luck, and the person who succeeded rarely checks. Investors who ride a rising market often believe they are skilled, then lose money when conditions change. Survivorship bias makes this worse. We study the companies that made it and miss the many that did the same things and failed.

## Putting the two together

The two work best as a pair. Success gives a target and a method, and failure corrects the method's flaws. Athletes, surgeons and pilots show this. They repeat what works, and they review their errors closely, often with a coach or a recorded replay. Aviation is the clearest case: the industry investigates every crash and near miss, and flying has become far safer as a result. Yet the safe flights are what make the system worth building.

What decides learning is reflection, not the outcome. A person who examines a success asks, "Which part was skill, and which was luck?" A person who examines a failure asks, "What exactly went wrong, and what would I change?" Someone who skips those questions learns little either way.

## Conclusion

If I have to choose, I say failure teaches more in any single moment, because it forces us to revise our beliefs. But a life made only of failure would be discouraging and would show us little of what good work looks like. The best learners treat both honestly. They study their failures without shame, and they question their successes without complacency. The outcome matters less than what the learner does with it afterward.
